blocks.text: A multiple allelic system occurs when a gene has more than two alternative forms (alleles) in a population, which creates more variation in a trait. Each person still carries only two of these alleles.
An example is the human ABO blood group system, controlled by one gene (the I gene) with three alleles: IA, IB and i. Different pairs of these alleles produce four blood groups.

blocks.caption: ABO blood groups and their genotypes

blocks.title: For information
blocks.text: In the ABO system the alleles IA and IB also show co-dominance. In Mendel's peas each character was controlled by a gene with two alleles, one completely dominant over the other; incomplete dominance and co-dominance do not follow this rule, and in a multiple allelic system a gene has more than two alleles, any two of which work together to produce a phenotype.

blocks.prompt: How many different genotypes are possible with the three ABO alleles?
blocks.explanation: Six: IA IA, IA i, IB IB, IB i, IA IB and i i, giving four phenotypes (A, B, AB, O).

items: Multiple alleles: more than two alleles in the population, two per person.
ABO: IA, IB, i; six genotypes, four groups.
